label: thm.alternating
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm.alternating}
Let $L$ be an alternating link with $\mu$ components. Then the Links--Gould polynomial of $L$ is alternating, namely,
\[
\mathrm{LG}(L;t_0,t_1)=\sum_{ij}(-1)^{\mu-1+i+j}|a_{ij}| t_0^it_1^j.
\]
Moreover, $\mathrm{LG}(L)\ne0$ if $L$ has a connected
alternating diagram.

label: thm.GHKST
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm.GHKST}
For $r=\pm1$ the operator $\mathrm{tr}_{2,\dots,n}\bigl((\mathrm{id}_W\otimes h^{\otimes(n-1)})\circ\varrho_r(w)\bigr)$ is a scalar multiple
of $\mathrm{id}_W$, and the scalar depends only on the oriented link $L=\widehat w$, the closure of $w$.
It is the $V_1$-polynomial $V_1(L)=V_1(L;t_0,t_1)$. In particular $V_1(\widehat w)=V(w;\pm1)$.

label: lem.twist
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $\varphi(i,j)=\beta(e_i)\alpha(e_j)$; thus $\varphi(3,2)=\varphi(3,4)=\varphi(4,2)=\varphi(4,4)=1$ and $\varphi(i,j)=0$
otherwise. The identity $R_r=F_rR_1F_r^{-1}$ says that the coefficient of $e_{kl}$ in $R_re_{ij}$ is
$r^{\varphi(k,l)-\varphi(i,j)}$ times its value at $r=1$. In \eqref{eq.R}--\eqref{eq.R2} the parameter $r$ occurs in
exactly eight coefficients, and one checks them one by one:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
e_{23}\mapsto e_{32}:\ \ r^{\varphi(3,2)-\varphi(2,3)}=r, &\qquad e_{32}\mapsto e_{23}:\ \ r^{-1},\\
e_{32}\mapsto e_{41}:\ \ r^{\varphi(4,1)-\varphi(3,2)}=r^{-1}, &\qquad e_{41}\mapsto e_{32}:\ \ r,\\
e_{24}\mapsto e_{42}:\ \ r^{\varphi(4,2)-\varphi(2,4)}=r, &\qquad e_{42}\mapsto e_{24}:\ \ r^{-1},\\
e_{34}\mapsto e_{43}:\ \ r^{\varphi(4,3)-\varphi(3,4)}=r^{-1}, &\qquad e_{43}\mapsto e_{34}:\ \ r,
\end{array}
\]
while for all other non-zero coefficients $\varphi(k,l)=\varphi(i,j)$ (for instance $\varphi(4,1)=\varphi(2,3)=\varphi(1,4)=0$).

Now let $F^{(n)}\in\mathrm{End}(W^{\otimes n})$ be the diagonal operator $F^{(n)}e_I=r^{\varphi_n(I)}e_I$ with
$\varphi_n(I)=\sum_{p<q}\beta(e_{m_p})\alpha(e_{m_q})$ for $I=(m_1,\dots,m_n)$. Fix $k$ and split
\begin{align*}
 \varphi_n(I)={}&\beta(e_{m_k})\alpha(e_{m_{k+1}})
   +\sum_{p<k}\beta(e_{m_p})\bigl(\alpha(e_{m_k})+\alpha(e_{m_{k+1}})\bigr)\\
   &+\sum_{q>k+1}\bigl(\beta(e_{m_k})+\beta(e_{m_{k+1}})\bigr)\alpha(e_{m_q})+(\text{terms without }m_k,m_{k+1}).
\end{align*}
The operator $\varrho_1(\sigma_k)$ changes only the $k$-th and $(k+1)$-st tensor factors and preserves their total
bidegree (Lemma~\ref{lem.blocks}); therefore only the first term changes, and
$F^{(n)}\varrho_1(\sigma_k^{\pm1})(F^{(n)})^{-1}=\mathrm{id}\otimes F_rR_1^{\pm1}F_r^{-1}\otimes\mathrm{id}=\varrho_r(\sigma_k^{\pm1})$.
Consequently $\varrho_r(w)=F^{(n)}\varrho_1(w)(F^{(n)})^{-1}$. Conjugation by a diagonal operator does not change
diagonal matrix entries, and $V(w;r)$ is a combination of diagonal entries of $\varrho_r(w)$.

body_md:

From now on $r=-1$, and we write $R=R_{-1}$, $\varrho=\varrho_{-1}$ and $V(w)=V(w;-1)$. By

closure. We keep the notation $V(w)$ for the state sum itself, as given by Definition~\ref{def.V}.

label: lem.minors
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Both sides are algebra endomorphisms that agree on $U$. \\
(ii) Let $S=\{s_1<\dots<s_k\}$. Expanding,
${\textstyle\bigwedge}(M)u_S=\sum_{p_1,\dots,p_k}M_{p_1s_1}\cdots M_{p_ks_k}\,u_{p_1}\wedge\dots\wedge u_{p_k}$.
A term vanishes unless the $p_m$ are distinct, and then $\{p_1,\dots,p_k\}=T=\{t_1<\dots<t_k\}$ with
$p_m=t_{\pi(m)}$ for a permutation $\pi$, and $u_{p_1}\wedge\dots\wedge u_{p_k}=\mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\,u_T$. The coefficient of
$u_T$ is therefore $\sum_\pi\mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\prod_mM_{t_{\pi(m)}s_m}=\det M[T|S]$.
head: environment

label: lem.str
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.str}
For $M\in\mathrm{End}(U)$,
\[
   \sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}}(-1)^{|S|}\,\bigl\langle u_S,{\textstyle\bigwedge}(M)u_S\bigr\rangle\;=\;\sum_{S}(-1)^{|S|}\det M[S|S]\;=\;\det(1-M).
\]
head: environment
name: the supertrace is a determinant

title: Proof
body_md:
The first equality is Lemma~\ref{lem.minors} (ii). The $q$-th column of $1-M$ is $u_q-Mu_q$. By multilinearity of
the determinant in the columns, $\det(1-M)=\sum_S(-1)^{|S|}\det C^S$, where the $q$-th column of $C^S$ is
$Mu_q$ if $q\in S$ and $u_q$ if $q\notin S$. Expanding $\det C^S$ along the columns $u_q$, $q\notin S$, gives
$\det C^S=\det M[S|S]$.
head: environment

label: lem.compress
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.compress}
Let $Q\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}$ and $M^\circ=M[Q|Q]$. Then
\[
   \sum_{S\subseteq Q}(-1)^{|S|}\,\langle u_S,{\textstyle\bigwedge}(M)u_S\rangle=\det(1-M^\circ).
\]
head: environment
name: compression

title: Proof
body_md:
For $S\subseteq Q$ we have $\langle u_S,{\textstyle\bigwedge}(M)u_S\rangle=\det M[S|S]=\det M^\circ[S|S]$; apply
Lemma~\ref{lem.str} to $M^\circ$.

label: lem.rankone
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.rankone}
Let $M\in\mathrm{End}(U)$, let $p$ be a column vector and $\ell^{\mathsf{T}}$ a row vector, and let $z$ be an indeterminate. Then
every matrix entry of ${\textstyle\bigwedge}(M+z\,p\ell^{\mathsf{T}})$ is a polynomial of degree $\le1$ in $z$. In particular
$\det(M+z\,p\ell^{\mathsf{T}})$ has degree $\le 1$ in $z$.
head: environment
name: rank-one perturbations

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem.minors} (ii) the entries are the minors $\det\bigl(M[T|S]+z\,p_T\ell_S^{\mathsf{T}}\bigr)$, where $p_T$,
$\ell_S$ are the restrictions of $p$, $\ell$. The $m$-th column of this matrix is (the $m$-th column of $M[T|S]$)
$+\,z\,\ell_{s_m}p_T$. Expanding by multilinearity, every term containing two or more columns proportional to
$p_T$ vanishes.

label: lem.fock
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.fock}
Let $n\ge1$.
\begin{enumerate}\renewcommand{\roman{enumi}}{\roman{enumi}}
\item $\Phi_n$ maps the basis $(e_I)$ bijectively onto the basis $(u_S)$ of $\mathcal F_n$; hence it is an isomorphism.
      For $I=(m_1,\dots,m_n)$ the element $\Phi_n(e_I)$ has degree $\sum_k\bigl(\alpha(e_{m_k})+\beta(e_{m_k})\bigr)$, and
      $\Phi_n(e_I)=u_S$ with $S\subseteq Q:=\{3,4,\dots,2n\}$ if and only if $m_1=1$.
\item \textup{(Locality)} Let $M_0\in\mathrm{End}(U_2)$ be a $4\times4$ matrix, let $1\le k\le n-1$, and let
      $M_0^{(k)}\in\mathrm{End}(U_n)$ act as $M_0$ on $(a_k,b_k,a_{k+1},b_{k+1})$ and as the identity on the other
      basis vectors. Then
      \[
         \Phi_n^{-1}\,{\textstyle\bigwedge}\bigl(M_0^{(k)}\bigr)\,\Phi_n=\mathrm{id}_W^{\otimes(k-1)}\otimes\bigl(\Phi_2^{-1}{\textstyle\bigwedge}(M_0)\Phi_2\bigr)\otimes\mathrm{id}_W^{\otimes(n-k-1)} .
      \]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) The wedge product in \eqref{eq.Phi} is a product of basis vectors $u_q$ with increasing indices, so it is
$u_S$ where $S$ records which of $a_k,b_k$ occur; conversely $S$ determines $I$. The rest is clear.

(ii) Write $\Phi_n(e_I)=\omega_<\wedge\omega_{\rm mid}\wedge\omega_>$, where $\omega_<$ is a product of the
$a_p,b_p$ with $p<k$, $\omega_>$ is a product of those with $p>k+1$, and
\[
   \omega_{\rm mid}=\omega_{m_k}(a_k,b_k)\wedge\omega_{m_{k+1}}(a_{k+1},b_{k+1}).
\]
Since ${\textstyle\bigwedge}(M_0^{(k)})$ is an algebra homomorphism which fixes the $a_p,b_p$ with $p\notin\{k,k+1\}$,
\[
  {\textstyle\bigwedge}\bigl(M_0^{(k)}\bigr)\bigl(\omega_<\wedge\omega_{\rm mid}\wedge\omega_>\bigr)
  =\omega_<\wedge{\textstyle\bigwedge}\bigl(M_0^{(k)}\bigr)(\omega_{\rm mid})\wedge\omega_> ,
\]
Moreover ${\textstyle\bigwedge}(M_0^{(k)})(\omega_{\rm mid})$ is obtained from ${\textstyle\bigwedge}(M_0)\Phi_2(e_{m_k}\otimes e_{m_{k+1}})$ by renaming
$a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2$ as $a_k,b_k,a_{k+1},b_{k+1}$. This is the claim.

label: cor.interaction

body_md:
\label{cor.interaction}
\begin{align*}
  \mathsf R&=\Phi_2^{-1}{\textstyle\bigwedge}\bigl(\rho(t_0)\oplus\rho(t_1)^{\mathsf{T}}\bigr)\Phi_2+(1-t_0t_1)\,D,\\
  \mathsf R^{-1}&=\Phi_2^{-1}{\textstyle\bigwedge}\bigl(\rho(t_0)^{-1}\oplus(\rho(t_1)^{\mathsf{T}})^{-1}\bigr)\Phi_2+\bigl(1-(t_0t_1)^{-1}\bigr)\,D^- ,
\end{align*}
where, with $X=c^{\dagger}_{a_1}(c_{a_1}-c_{a_2})=n_{a_1}-c^{\dagger}_{a_1}c_{a_2}$ and $Y=(c^{\dagger}_{b_1}-c^{\dagger}_{b_2})c_{b_1}=n_{b_1}-c^{\dagger}_{b_2}c_{b_1}$,
\[
   D=\Phi_2^{-1}\,XY\,\Phi_2,\qquad D^-=\Phi_2^{-1}\,X^-Y^-\,\Phi_2,\qquad
   X^-=n_{a_2}-c^{\dagger}_{a_2}c_{a_1},\quad Y^-=n_{b_2}-c^{\dagger}_{b_1}c_{b_2}.
\]
In particular $\mathsf R$ is of the form $\Phi_2^{-1}{\textstyle\bigwedge}(M_0)\Phi_2$ at $t_0t_1=1$.
head: environment
name: the quartic term

title: Proof
body_md:
The two displayed formulas are Theorem~\ref{thm.A} combined with the second expression in \eqref{eq.E1} and
with \eqref{eq.Ginv}, which gives $G^{-}(t_0^{-1},t_1^{-1})=G(t_0,t_1)^{-1}$. For the operator form, note that $X$
involves only $a_1,a_2$ and $Y$ only $b_1,b_2$, and that on monomials
\begin{align*}
  X\colon&\quad 1\mapsto0,\quad a_1\mapsto a_1,\quad a_2\mapsto-a_1,\quad a_1\wedge a_2\mapsto a_1\wedge a_2;\\
  Y\colon&\quad 1\mapsto0,\quad b_1\mapsto b_1-b_2,\quad b_2\mapsto0,\quad b_1\wedge b_2\mapsto b_1\wedge b_2 .
\end{align*}
Moreover $XY(\mu\wedge\nu)=X(\mu)\wedge Y(\nu)$ for monomials $\mu$ in $a_1,a_2$ and $\nu$ in $b_1,b_2$ (moving
$c_{b_1}$ and then $c^{\dagger}_{b_1}$ or $c^{\dagger}_{b_2}$ across $\mu$ produces the sign $(-1)^{|\mu|}$ twice). Writing the six relevant
basis vectors as $\pm\mu\wedge\nu$,
\[
\begin{gathered}
\Phi_2(e_{41})=a_1\wedge b_1,\quad \Phi_2(e_{32})=-a_2\wedge b_1,\quad \Phi_2(e_{42})=-a_1\wedge a_2\wedge b_1,\\
\Phi_2(e_{43})=a_1\wedge b_1\wedge b_2,\quad \Phi_2(e_{34})=-a_2\wedge b_1\wedge b_2,\quad \Phi_2(e_{44})=-a_1\wedge a_2\wedge b_1\wedge b_2,
\end{gathered}
\]
we get $XY\Phi_2(e_{41})=a_1\wedge(b_1-b_2)=\Phi_2(e_{41}-e_{23})$,
$XY\Phi_2(e_{32})=a_1\wedge(b_1-b_2)$,
$XY\Phi_2(e_{42})=-a_1\wedge a_2\wedge(b_1-b_2)=\Phi_2(e_{42}+e_{24})$,
$XY\Phi_2(e_{43})=\Phi_2(e_{43})$, $XY\Phi_2(e_{34})=a_1\wedge b_1\wedge b_2=\Phi_2(e_{43})$ and
$XY\Phi_2(e_{44})=\Phi_2(e_{44})$; on the other ten basis vectors $X$ or $Y$ vanishes. This is \eqref{eq.D}.
The computation for $D^-$ is the same with the two strands exchanged:
$X^-\colon a_2\mapsto a_2$, $a_1\mapsto-a_2$, $a_1\wedge a_2\mapsto a_1\wedge a_2$ and
$Y^-\colon b_2\mapsto b_2-b_1$, $b_1\mapsto0$, $b_1\wedge b_2\mapsto b_1\wedge b_2$.

label: rem.ffc
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem.ffc}
For one flavor, the Kauffman--Saleur free-fermion condition \cite[(5.3)]{KauffmanSaleur} says precisely that the vertex
operator, normalised so that the empty vertex has weight $1$, is ${\textstyle\bigwedge}$ of its restriction to one-particle states
\cite[(5.2)--(5.5)]{KauffmanSaleur}. By Table~\ref{tab.Rp} the restriction of $\mathsf R$ to
one-particle states is $\rho(t_0)\oplus\rho(t_1)^{\mathsf{T}}$, so Corollary~\ref{cor.interaction} measures the failure of the
free-fermion condition: it is the operator $(1-t_0t_1)D$ of rank $4$. For instance the doubly occupied
configuration $e_{44}\mapsto e_{44}$ has weight $1$ instead of $\det\rho(t_0)\det\rho(t_1)=t_0t_1$.

title: Remark

\label{rem.Lambda1}
The operator $\Phi_2^{-1}{\textstyle\bigwedge}(\rho(t_0)\oplus\rho(t_1))\Phi_2$ is the free two-flavor $R$-matrix; by
Lemma~\ref{lem.str} its braid closures give products of two Burau determinants, i.e.\

label: thm.B
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq.VV1} it suffices to prove the formula for the state sum $V(w)$. We do this in three steps.

\smallskip\emph{Step 1: one crossing.} Let $K_n\in\mathrm{End}(W^{\otimes n})$ be the diagonal operator
\[
   K_ne_I=t_1^{\sum_k(k-1)\beta(e_{m_k})}\,e_I\qquad\text{for }I=(m_1,\dots,m_n),
\]
and let $\mathbbm B_j=B_j(x_j)\oplus\widetilde{B}_j(y_j)\in\mathrm{End}(U_n)$ in the notation of Section~\ref{ssec.fock}. We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq.step1}
   -K_n\,\varrho(s_j)\,K_n^{-1}=\Phi_n^{-1}\ \mathbbm E_{t_0^{\varepsilon_j},\,t_1^{\varepsilon_j}}\bigl[{\textstyle\bigwedge}(\mathbbm B_j)\bigr]\ \Phi_n .
\end{equation}
Let $i=\nu_j$. The exponent of $t_1$ in $K_ne_I$ is
$(i-1)\bigl(\beta(e_{m_i})+\beta(e_{m_{i+1}})\bigr)+\beta(e_{m_{i+1}})$ plus terms not involving the $i$-th and
$(i+1)$-st tensor factors. Since $R^{\pm1}$ preserves the total $\beta$-degree of these two factors
(Lemma~\ref{lem.blocks}), we get $K_n\varrho(\sigma_i^{\pm1})K_n^{-1}=\mathrm{id}\otimes KR^{\pm1}K^{-1}\otimes\mathrm{id}$ with $K$ as in
\eqref{eq.K}, that is, $-K_n\varrho(\sigma_i^{\pm1})K_n^{-1}=\mathrm{id}\otimes\mathsf R^{\pm1}\otimes\mathrm{id}$. By
Theorem~\ref{thm.A}, $\mathsf R=\mathbbm E_{t_0,t_1}[G(x_j,y_j)]$ and $\mathsf R^{-1}=\mathbbm E_{t_0^{-1},t_1^{-1}}[G^{-}(x_j,y_j)]$. Finally,
by the locality Lemma~\ref{lem.fock} (ii) applied to $M_0=\rho^{\pm}(x_j)\oplus\rho^{\pm}(y_j)^{\mathsf{T}}$,
\[
  \mathrm{id}^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimesG(x_j,y_j)\otimes\mathrm{id}^{\otimes(n-i-1)}=\Phi_n^{-1}{\textstyle\bigwedge}\bigl(M_0^{(i)}\bigr)\Phi_n ,\qquad M_0^{(i)}=B_j(x_j)\oplus\widetilde{B}_j(y_j)=\mathbbm B_j
\]
for $\varepsilon_j=+1$, and the same with $G^{-}$ for $\varepsilon_j=-1$. This proves \eqref{eq.step1}.

\smallskip\emph{Step 2: the whole braid.} Multiplying the identities \eqref{eq.step1} for $j=c,\dots,1$,
\begin{align*}
  (-1)^cK_n\,\varrho(w)\,K_n^{-1}
  &=\Phi_n^{-1}\ \mathbbm E_{t_0^{\varepsilon_c},t_1^{\varepsilon_c}}\bigl[{\textstyle\bigwedge}(\mathbbm B_c)\bigr]\cdots\mathbbm E_{t_0^{\varepsilon_1},t_1^{\varepsilon_1}}\bigl[{\textstyle\bigwedge}(\mathbbm B_1)\bigr]\ \Phi_n\\
  &=\Phi_n^{-1}\ \mathbbm E\bigl[{\textstyle\bigwedge}(\mathbbm B_c)\cdots{\textstyle\bigwedge}(\mathbbm B_1)\bigr]\ \Phi_n .
\end{align*}
The second equality is \eqref{eq.Emult}, applied to each matrix entry of the product: such an entry is a sum of
products of one entry from each factor, and the entries of ${\textstyle\bigwedge}(\mathbbm B_j)$ have degree $\le1$ in $x_j$ and in $y_j$
and involve no other variable. By Lemma~\ref{lem.minors} (i),
${\textstyle\bigwedge}(\mathbbm B_c)\cdots{\textstyle\bigwedge}(\mathbbm B_1)={\textstyle\bigwedge}(\mathbbm B)$ with $\mathbbm B=\mathbbm B_c\cdots\mathbbm B_1=B(x)\oplus\widetilde{B}(y)$. So
\begin{equation}\label{eq.step2}
   (-1)^cK_n\,\varrho(w)\,K_n^{-1}=\Phi_n^{-1}\ \mathbbm E\bigl[{\textstyle\bigwedge}\bigl(B(x)\oplus\widetilde{B}(y)\bigr)\bigr]\ \Phi_n .
\end{equation}

\smallskip\emph{Step 3: the closure.} Conjugation by the diagonal operator $K_n$ does not change diagonal matrix
entries. By Lemma~\ref{lem.fock} (i), the vectors $e_{(1,m_2,\dots,m_n)}$ correspond under $\Phi_n$ to the $u_S$ with
$S\subseteq Q=\{3,\dots,2n\}$, and by \eqref{eq.hparity} $h_{m_2}\cdots h_{m_n}=(-1)^{n-1}(-1)^{|S|}$. Therefore, by
Definition~\ref{def.V} and \eqref{eq.step2},
\[
   V(w)=(-1)^{n-1+c}\sum_{S\subseteq Q}(-1)^{|S|}\,\mathbbm E\bigl[\langle u_S,{\textstyle\bigwedge}(\mathbbm B)u_S\rangle\bigr]
       =(-1)^{n-1+c}\,\mathbbm E\bigl[\det\bigl(1-\mathbbm B[Q|Q]\bigr)\bigr]
\]
by Lemma~\ref{lem.compress} and the linearity of $\mathbbm E$, and
$\det(1-\mathbbm B[Q|Q])=\det(1-B(x)')\det(1-\widetilde{B}(y)')=P_w(x)\widetilde{P}_w(y)$ by \eqref{eq.detsum}. This is the asserted formula
for $V(w)$.

label: rem.reverse
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem.reverse}
Let $w^{\rm rev}=s_c\cdots s_2s_1$ be the reversed word, with its crossings numbered so that the crossing $j$ is still
the letter $s_j$. By \eqref{eq.B},
\begin{align*}
   B_{w^{\rm rev}}(x)&=B_1(x_1)B_2(x_2)\cdots B_c(x_c)=\widetilde{B}_w(x)^{\mathsf{T}},\\
   \widetilde{B}_{w^{\rm rev}}(y)&=\widetilde{B}_1(y_1)\widetilde{B}_2(y_2)\cdots\widetilde{B}_c(y_c)=B_w(y)^{\mathsf{T}},
\end{align*}
and deleting the first row and column commutes with transposition, so $P_{w^{\rm rev}}=\widetilde{P}_w$ and
$\widetilde{P}_{w^{\rm rev}}=P_w$. The closure of $w^{\rm rev}$ is the closure $L$ of $w$ with the orientation of all components
reversed; we denote it by $-L$.
Theorem~\ref{thm.B} for $w^{\rm rev}$, with the names of the variables $x$ and $y$ exchanged, therefore gives
\[
   V_1(-L;t_0,t_1)=V_1(L;t_1,t_0).
\]
Thus the symmetry
$V_1(L;t_0,t_1)=V_1(L;t_1,t_0)$ is equivalent to the invariance of $V_1$ under reversal of the orientation. This is consistent since the Links--Gould invariant does not distinguish a link from its inverse \cite{DeWitKauffmanLinks},
and $V_1$ is the Links--Gould invariant \cite{GHKKST}. In particular the direction in which braid words are read
(Section~\ref{sec.setup}) is immaterial for the value of $V_1$.

name: reversing the word

label: ex.unknot
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex.unknot}
For $w=\sigma_1$ ($n=2$): $B=\rho(x_1)$, $B'=(0)$, so $P_w=\widetilde{P}_w=1$ and $V_1=1$.
For $w=\sigma_1^{-1}$: $B=\rho^-(x_1)$, $B'=(1-x_1)$, so $P_w=x_1$, $\widetilde{P}_w=y_1$, and
$V_1=\mathbbm E[x_1y_1]=1$. Here the two Burau determinants alone would give $t_0^{-1}t_1^{-1}$; the rule
$x_1y_1\mapsto1$ is what makes the formula invariant under the Markov III move.
head: environment
name: unknots

title: Example
body_md:
$w=\sigma_1^2$, $n=2$, $\mu=2$. $B=\rho(x_2)\rho(x_1)$ has lower right entry $x_1$, so $P_w=1-x_1$; similarly
$\widetilde{P}_w=1-y_2$. No crossing contributes both variables, and $V_1=-(1-t_0)(1-t_1)$.
head: environment
name: Hopf link

label: ex.trefoil
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex.trefoil}
$w=\sigma_1^3$, $n=2$. The lower right entries of $\rho(x_3)\rho(x_2)\rho(x_1)$ and of
$\rho(y_3)^{\mathsf{T}}\rho(y_2)^{\mathsf{T}}\rho(y_1)^{\mathsf{T}}$ are $x_1(1-x_2)$ and $y_3(1-y_2)$, so
\[
   P_w=1-x_1+x_1x_2,\qquad \widetilde{P}_w=1-y_3+y_2y_3 .
\]
The only monomial of $P_w\widetilde{P}_w$ containing a product $x_jy_j$ is $x_1x_2\cdot y_2y_3\mapsto t_0t_1$ (instead of
$t_0^2t_1^2$). Hence
\[
   V_1(3_1)=(1-t_0+t_0^2)(1-t_1+t_1^2)+t_0t_1(1-t_0t_1)
           =1-t_0-t_1+t_0^2+t_1^2+2t_0t_1-t_0^2t_1-t_0t_1^2 .
\]
head: environment
name: trefoil

title: Example
body_md:
$w=\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}$, $n=3$. One finds
\[
   P_w=x_2+x_4-x_1x_4-x_2x_4+x_1x_2x_4,\qquad \widetilde{P}_w=y_2+y_4-y_2y_4-y_3y_4+y_2y_3y_4 ,
\]
and, with $\mathbbm E[x_1]=t_0$, $\mathbbm E[x_2]=\mathbbm E[x_4]=t_0^{-1}$, $\mathbbm E[y_3]=t_1$, $\mathbbm E[y_2]=\mathbbm E[y_4]=t_1^{-1}$, $\mathbbm E[x_jy_j]=1$,
\[
  V_1(4_1)=7-3\bigl(t_0+t_1+t_0^{-1}+t_1^{-1}\bigr)+2\bigl(t_0t_1+t_0^{-1}t_1^{-1}\bigr)+t_0t_1^{-1}+t_0^{-1}t_1 .
\]
head: environment
name: figure-eight knot

label: cor.expansion
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor.expansion}
Write $P_w(\bar x+\delta)=\sum_{S}a_S\,\delta^S$ and $\widetilde{P}_w(\bar y+\delta')=\sum_Sb_S\,\delta'^S$ with
$a_S\in\mathbbm Z[t_0^{\pm1}]$, $b_S\in\mathbbm Z[t_1^{\pm1}]$, the sums running over $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,c\}$. Then
\[
   V_1(L;t_0,t_1)=(-1)^{\mu-1}\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,c\}}\ \Bigl(\prod_{j\in S}g_j\Bigr)\,a_S\,b_S .
\]
The term $S=\emptyset$ is $P_w(\bar x)\widetilde{P}_w(\bar y)$, the product of the two ordinary Burau determinants at $t_0$ and
$t_1$; all other terms are divisible by $1-t_0t_1$.
head: environment
name: expansion around the free theory

title: Proof
body_md:
With $x_j=\bar x_j+\delta_j$, $y_j=\bar y_j+\delta'_j$ we have $\mathbbm E[\delta_j]=\mathbbm E[\delta'_j]=0$ and
$\mathbbm E[\delta_j\delta'_j]=\mathbbm E[x_jy_j]-\bar x_j\bar y_j=g_j$. By \eqref{eq.Emult},
$\mathbbm E[\delta^S\delta'^{S'}]=\prod_{j\in S}g_j$ if $S=S'$ and $0$ otherwise. Hence
$\mathbbm E[P_w(x)\widetilde{P}_w(y)]=\sum_S\bigl(\prod_{j\in S}g_j\bigr)a_Sb_S$, and the claim follows from Theorem~\ref{thm.B}.
head: environment

label: rem.burau
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem.burau}
If $t_0t_1=1$ then all $g_j$ vanish and
$V_1(L;t,t^{-1})=(-1)^{\mu-1}P_w(t^{\varepsilon})\,\widetilde{P}_w(t^{-\varepsilon})$, a product of two Burau determinants. By the classical
theorem of Burau, $\det(1-B')$ at $x_j=t^{\varepsilon_j}$ equals the Alexander polynomial up to a
unit. More precisely, let $\Delta_L(t)=\nabla_L(t^{1/2}-t^{-1/2})$ be the Conway-normalised Alexander polynomial; it
satisfies $\Delta_L(t^{-1})=(-1)^{\mu-1}\Delta_L(t)$. Then
$P_w(t^{\varepsilon})=(-1)^{\mu-1}\,t^{(e-n+1)/2}\Delta_L(t)$ with $e=\sum_j\varepsilon_j$, the letters $\sigma_i$ being positive
crossings. Moreover $\widetilde{P}_w(t^{\varepsilon})=P_w(t^{\varepsilon})$: indeed $\rho(t)^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathrm{diag}(1,t)\rho(t)\mathrm{diag}(1,t)^{-1}$, and the same holds
for $\rho^-(t^{-1})=\rho(t)^{-1}$; hence
$\widetilde{B}(t^\varepsilon)=T\,B(t^\varepsilon)\,T^{-1}$ with $T=\mathrm{diag}(1,t,\dots,t^{n-1})$, and conjugation by a diagonal matrix commutes
with deleting the first row and column. So one recovers
$V_1(L;t,t^{-1})=(-1)^{\mu-1}\Delta_L(t)\Delta_L(t^{-1})=\Delta_L(t)^2$ \cite{Kohli}, and
Corollary~\ref{cor.expansion} says
\[
     V_1(L;t_0,t_1)=(-1)^{\mu-1}\,P_w(t_0^{\varepsilon})\,P_w(t_1^{\varepsilon})+(1-t_0t_1)(\cdots),\qquad
   P_w(t^{\varepsilon})=(-1)^{\mu-1}\,t^{(e-n+1)/2}\Delta_L(t).
\]
head: environment
name: the free point and the Alexander polynomial

label: lem.cyclic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.cyclic}
Let $C_1,\dots,C_c$ be $n\times n$ matrices. Let $\mathcal C$ be the $nc\times nc$ matrix, with rows and columns
indexed by pairs $(p,j)$, $1\le p\le n$, $j\in\mathbbm Z/c$, defined by
$\mathcal C[(p',j+1),(p,j)]=(C_j)_{p'p}$ and $\mathcal C[(p',j'),(p,j)]=0$ if $j'\ne j+1$. Then
\[
   \det(1-\mathcal C)=\det(1-C_cC_{c-1}\cdots C_1).
\]
head: environment
name: cyclic products

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the identity $\det\begin{psmallmatrix}A&B\\D&1\end{psmallmatrix}=\det(A-BD)$ for block matrices, which
follows from
$\begin{psmallmatrix}A&B\\D&1\end{psmallmatrix}\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\-D&1\end{psmallmatrix}
=\begin{psmallmatrix}A-BD&B\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$. For $c=1$ there is nothing to prove. Let $c\ge2$ and order the
index set so that the level $j=2$ comes last. In the corresponding block form of $1-\mathcal C$, the last diagonal
block is $1$, the block $D$ (rows of level $2$) has the single non-zero entry $-C_1$ in the columns of level $1$,
and the block $B$ (columns of level $2$) has the single non-zero entry $-C_2$ in the rows of level $3$ (level $1$
if $c=2$). Hence $A-BD$ is $1-\mathcal C^\flat$, where $\mathcal C^\flat$ is the matrix of the same kind built from
the $c-1$ matrices $C_2C_1,C_3,\dots,C_c$. The claim follows by induction on $c$.
head: environment

label: lem.merge
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.merge}
Let $Z$ be a square matrix with rows and columns indexed by a finite set $\mathcal N$, and let $\xi\ne\zeta$ in $\mathcal N$ be
such that the column $\xi$ of $Z$ and the row $\zeta$ of $Z$ both have the single non-zero entry $Z[\zeta,\xi]=1$.
Let $Z^\flat$ be the matrix indexed by $\mathcal N\smallsetminus\{\zeta\}$ with
\[
   Z^\flat[k,l]=Z[k,l]\ \ (l\ne\xi),\qquad Z^\flat[k,\xi]=Z[k,\zeta].
\]
Then $\det(1-Z)=\det(1-Z^\flat)$. Moreover, if $d\in\mathcal N$ and the subscript $\hat d$ denotes deletion of the row and
column $d$, then $\det\bigl((1-Z)_{\hat d}\bigr)=\det\bigl((1-Z^\flat)_{\hat d}\bigr)$ for $d\notin\{\xi,\zeta\}$, and
$\det\bigl((1-Z)_{\hat d}\bigr)=\det\bigl((1-Z^\flat)_{\hat\xi}\bigr)$ for $d\in\{\xi,\zeta\}$.
head: environment
name: merging two nodes

title: Proof
body_md:
The row $\zeta$ of $1-Z$ has the entries $1$ in column $\zeta$ and $-1$ in column $\xi$, and zeros elsewhere. Adding
column $\zeta$ to column $\xi$ does not change the determinant and makes row $\zeta$ equal to the $\zeta$-th unit row;
expanding along it removes row and column $\zeta$. For $k\ne\zeta$ the new entry in position $(k,\xi)$ is
$(\delta_{k\xi}-Z[k,\xi])+(\delta_{k\zeta}-Z[k,\zeta])=\delta_{k\xi}-Z[k,\zeta]$, because $Z[k,\xi]=0$ for $k\ne\zeta$. This is
$(1-Z^\flat)[k,\xi]$, which proves the first claim. For $d\notin\{\xi,\zeta\}$ the same argument applies to the
matrices with row and column $d$ deleted. If $d=\xi$: in $(1-Z)_{\hat\xi}$ the row $\zeta$ is the $\zeta$-th unit row,
and expanding along it gives the determinant of $1-Z$ with rows and columns $\xi,\zeta$ deleted, which is
$(1-Z^\flat)_{\hat\xi}$. If $d=\zeta$: in $(1-Z)_{\hat\zeta}$ the column $\xi$ is the $\xi$-th unit column, with the
same conclusion.

label: def.T
title: Definition
head: environment

label: prop.edge
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop.edge}
With the notation above,
\[
   P_w(x)=\det\bigl((1-T^a(x))_{\hat e}\bigr),\qquad \widetilde{P}_w(y)=\det\bigl((1-T^b(y))_{\hat e}\bigr),
\]
where the subscript $\hat e$ denotes deletion of the row and column of the edge $\hat e$. Consequently
\[
   V_1(L;t_0,t_1)=(-1)^{\mu-1}\ \mathbbm E\Bigl[\det\bigl((1-T^a(x))_{\hat e}\bigr)\,\det\bigl((1-T^b(y))_{\hat e}\bigr)\Bigr].
\]
head: environment
name: edge form

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Step 1.} Let $\mathbbm T^\circ$ be $\mathbbm T(x)$ with the row and the column of the node $(1,1)$ replaced by zero. Then
$\det((1-\mathbbm T(x))_{\widehat{(1,1)}})=\det(1-\mathbbm T^\circ)$ (expand along the row $(1,1)$ of $1-\mathbbm T^\circ$, which is a
unit row). The matrix $\mathbbm T^\circ$ is of the form considered in Lemma~\ref{lem.cyclic}, with $C_1=B_1\Pi$,
$C_c=\Pi B_c$ ($C_1=\Pi B_1\Pi$ if $c=1$) and $C_j=B_j$ otherwise, where $\Pi=\mathrm{diag}(0,1,\dots,1)$. Hence
\[
  \det\bigl((1-\mathbbm T(x))_{\widehat{(1,1)}}\bigr)=\det\bigl(1-\Pi\,B(x)\,\Pi\bigr)=\det\bigl(1-B(x)'\bigr)=P_w(x),
\]
because $\Pi B(x)\Pi=0\oplus B(x)'$.

\emph{Step 2.} If $(p,j)$ is a passive node, then $\xi=(p,j)$ and $\zeta=(p,j+1)$ satisfy the hypothesis of
Lemma~\ref{lem.merge} for $Z=\mathbbm T(x)$. Merging $\zeta$ into $\xi$ produces a matrix indexed by
$\mathcal N\smallsetminus\{\zeta\}$ in which $\xi$ has inherited the column of $\zeta$; if $\zeta$ was itself passive, the pair
$(\xi,(p,j+2))$ again satisfies
the hypothesis, and the hypothesis for all other passive nodes is unaffected. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem.merge}
successively to all passive nodes, each edge (a chain of nodes) is merged into its first node, which inherits the
column of its last, active, node. The resulting matrix is indexed by the edges, and its entry in row $e'$ and
column $e$ is $\mathbbm T(x)[(\text{first node of }e'),(\text{last node of }e)]$, i.e.\ the sum over the crossings $j$
which $e$ enters and $e'$ leaves of the corresponding entry of the block $\rho^{\varepsilon_j}(x_j)$ of $B_j(x_j)$, whose
rows correspond to $(\mathrm{out}_L,\mathrm{out}_R)$ and columns to $(\mathrm{in}_L,\mathrm{in}_R)$. Comparing
\[
  \rho(x)=\bordermatrix{&\scriptstyle o&\scriptstyle u\cr \scriptstyle u'&1-x&x\cr \scriptstyle o'&1&0},\qquad
  \rho^-(x)=\bordermatrix{&\scriptstyle u&\scriptstyle o\cr \scriptstyle o'&0&1\cr \scriptstyle u'&x&1-x}
\]
with \eqref{eq.ou} and Definition~\ref{def.T}, this matrix is $T^a(x)$. By the last part of Lemma~\ref{lem.merge},
the deleted node $(1,1)$ becomes the deleted edge $\hat e$. Thus
$\det((1-T^a(x))_{\hat e})=\det((1-\mathbbm T(x))_{\widehat{(1,1)}})=P_w(x)$.

\emph{Step 3.} The same argument applies to $\widetilde\mathbbm T(y)$, whose blocks are the transposed matrices
\[
  \rho(y)^{\mathsf{T}}=\bordermatrix{&\scriptstyle o&\scriptstyle u\cr \scriptstyle u'&1-y&1\cr \scriptstyle o'&y&0},\qquad
  \rho^-(y)^{\mathsf{T}}=\bordermatrix{&\scriptstyle u&\scriptstyle o\cr \scriptstyle o'&0&y\cr \scriptstyle u'&1&1-y},
\]
and gives $T^b(y)$. The last assertion is Theorem~\ref{thm.B}.
head: environment

label: lem.gauss
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.gauss}
For every matrix $A=(A_{kl})_{k,l\in\mathcal K}$ with entries in $\mathbbm K$,
\[
   \int\exp\Bigl(\sum_{k,l\in\mathcal K}\psi_k\,A_{kl}\,\psi^+_l\Bigr)=\det A .
\]
head: environment
name: Gaussian integral

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $\theta_k=\sum_lA_{kl}\psi_l^+$. The elements $\psi_k\theta_k$ are even and $(\psi_k\theta_k)^2=0$, so
$\exp(\sum_k\psi_k\theta_k)=\prod_k(1+\psi_k\theta_k)$, and its component of top degree $2N$ is
$\prod_k\psi_k\theta_k$. Number $\mathcal K=\{1,\dots,N\}$. Then
\[
  \prod_{k=1}^N\psi_k\theta_k=\sum_{l_1,\dots,l_N}A_{1l_1}\cdots A_{Nl_N}\ \psi_1\psi^+_{l_1}\psi_2\psi^+_{l_2}\cdots\psi_N\psi^+_{l_N},
\]
and a term vanishes unless $k\mapsto l_k$ is a permutation $\pi$. Moving all $\psi$'s to the left costs a sign
$s_N$ which does not depend on $\pi$, so
\begin{align*}
 \psi_1\psi^+_{\pi(1)}\cdots\psi_N\psi^+_{\pi(N)}&=s_N\,\psi_1\cdots\psi_N\,\psi^+_{\pi(1)}\cdots\psi^+_{\pi(N)}
   =s_N\,\mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\,\psi_1\cdots\psi_N\,\psi^+_{1}\cdots\psi^+_{N}\\
   &=\mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\,\psi_1\psi_1^+\cdots\psi_N\psi_N^+ .
\end{align*}
Hence the integral is $\sum_\pi\mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\prod_kA_{k\pi(k)}=\det A$.

label: lem.nil
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.nil}
Let $p=(p_k)$ and $\ell=(\ell_k)$ be vectors indexed by $\mathcal K$ and
\[
   X=\Bigl(\sum_kp_k\psi_k\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{k'}\ell_{k'}\psi_{k'}^+\Bigr).
\]
Then $X$ is even, $X^2=0$, and $\exp(zX)=1+zX$ for every scalar $z$. Moreover, for every matrix $A$ indexed by
$\mathcal K$,
\[
   \sum_{k,k'}\psi_k\bigl(A-z\,p\ell^{\mathsf{T}}\bigr)_{kk'}\psi_{k'}^+=\sum_{k,k'}\psi_kA_{kk'}\psi^+_{k'}-zX .
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: $X=\theta\theta'$ with $\theta,\theta'$ of degree one, and $\theta\theta'\theta\theta'=-\theta^2\theta'^2=0$. The last statement is clear.
head: environment

label: thm.C
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm.C}
With the notation above,
\[
   V_1(L;t_0,t_1)=(-1)^{\mu-1}\int\exp\Bigl(\mathcal S_a+\mathcal S_b+\sum_{j=1}^cg_j\,X_jY_j\Bigr).
\]
Explicitly, the interaction is the
sum over the crossings of the quartic vertices
\[
   \bigl(1-(t_0t_1)^{\varepsilon_j}\bigr)\ \psi^a_{u'_j}\bigl(\psi^{a+}_{u_j}-\psi^{a+}_{o_j}\bigr)\bigl(\psi^b_{o'_j}-\psi^b_{u'_j}\bigr)\psi^{b+}_{o_j}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_c,\delta'_1,\dots,\delta'_c$ be indeterminates. By \eqref{eq.rank1} and Lemma~\ref{lem.nil},
\[
  \sum_{e,e'}\psi^a_e\bigl(1-T^a(\bar x+\delta)\bigr)_{ee'}\psi^{a+}_{e'}=\mathcal S_a-\sum_j\delta_jX_j,\qquad
  \sum_{e,e'}\psi^b_e\bigl(1-T^b(\bar y+\delta')\bigr)_{ee'}\psi^{b+}_{e'}=\mathcal S_b-\sum_j\delta'_jY_j .
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem.gauss} to the index set $\mathcal K=\{a,b\}\times\{e\ne\hat e\}$ and to the block diagonal matrix
with blocks $(1-T^a(\bar x+\delta))_{\hat e}$ and $(1-T^b(\bar y+\delta'))_{\hat e}$ (the lemma and its proof hold over the
polynomial ring $\mathbbm K[\delta,\delta']$); by Proposition~\ref{prop.edge} its determinant is $P_w(\bar x+\delta)\,\widetilde{P}_w(\bar y+\delta')$. Since the $X_j,Y_j$ are even with square zero (Lemma~\ref{lem.nil}), we get
\[
   \int\exp(\mathcal S_a+\mathcal S_b)\ \prod_{j=1}^c(1-\delta_jX_j)(1-\delta'_jY_j)\;=\;P_w(\bar x+\delta)\,\widetilde{P}_w(\bar y+\delta') ,
\]
an identity between polynomials in $\delta,\delta'$. Comparing the coefficients of $\delta^S\delta'^S$ for $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,c\}$
gives $\int\exp(\mathcal S_a+\mathcal S_b)\prod_{j\in S}X_jY_j=a_Sb_S$ in the notation of Corollary~\ref{cor.expansion}. Multiplying
by $\prod_{j\in S}g_j$ and summing over $S$,
\[
  \int\exp(\mathcal S_a+\mathcal S_b)\prod_{j=1}^c(1+g_jX_jY_j)=\sum_S\Bigl(\prod_{j\in S}g_j\Bigr)a_Sb_S=(-1)^{\mu-1}\,V_1(L;t_0,t_1)
\]
by Corollary~\ref{cor.expansion}. Finally $\prod_j(1+g_jX_jY_j)=\exp(\sum_jg_jX_jY_j)$, because the $X_jY_j$ are even
and $(X_jY_j)^2=0$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Without the vertices, Theorem~\ref{thm.C} is the Gaussian integral of \cite[(6.13)]{KauffmanSaleur} taken once for each
flavor, with value $P_w(\bar x)\widetilde{P}_w(\bar y)$, up to the normalisation of the vertex weights (Kauffman and Saleur use a
symmetric normalisation of the Burau weights and a global prefactor). There are two further differences of
presentation. Kauffman and Saleur label their
Grassmann variables by the pairs (crossing, strand through this crossing) rather than by the edges. And they keep
the variables at the two ends of the edge where the diagram is cut open, omitting only the propagator of this edge,
so that their matrix has size $2c$ instead of $2c-1$. In the present notation this amounts to replacing
$(1-T^\sigma)_{\hat e}$ by $1-T^\sigma-E_{\hat e\hat e}$, and
$\det(1-T^\sigma-E_{\hat e\hat e})=\det(1-T^\sigma)-\det((1-T^\sigma)_{\hat e})=-\det((1-T^\sigma)_{\hat e})$, because
$\det(1-T^\sigma)=0$ (the rows of $T^a$ and the columns of $T^b$ have sum $1$). So the two flavors are free
``Alexander fermions'' at $t_0$ and $t_1$, coupled only by a contact interaction at the crossings, of strength
$1-(t_0t_1)^{\pm1}$.

label: lem.mtt
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.mtt}
Let $Z$ be a square matrix with rows and columns indexed by a finite set $\mathcal N$, with entries in a commutative ring,
and let $d\in\mathcal N$. Assume that $\sum_{l\in\mathcal N}Z[k,l]=1$ for every $k\ne d$. Call a map
$f\colon\mathcal N\smallsetminus\{d\}\to\mathcal N$ a \emph{tree rooted at $d$} if every $k\ne d$ is mapped to $d$ by some
iterate of $f$. Then, with the notation of Lemma~\ref{lem.merge},
\[
   \det\bigl((1-Z)_{\hat d}\bigr)=\sum_{f}\ \prod_{k\ne d}Z[k,f(k)] ,
\]
where the sum runs over all trees rooted at $d$.
head: environment
name: matrix-tree theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $\mathcal N^\circ=\mathcal N\smallsetminus\{d\}$ and $A=(1-Z)_{\hat d}$. For $k\ne l$ in $\mathcal N^\circ$ we have $A[k,l]=-Z[k,l]$,
and by the assumption on the row sums
\[
   A[k,k]=1-Z[k,k]=\sum_{l\in\mathcal N,\ l\ne k}Z[k,l]\qquad(k\in\mathcal N^\circ).
\]
Expand $\det A=\sum_\sigma\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{k\in\mathcal N^\circ}A[k,\sigma(k)]$ over the permutations $\sigma$ of
$\mathcal N^\circ$. A cycle $(k_1\,k_2\,\cdots\,k_m)$ of $\sigma$ of length $m\ge2$ contributes the sign $(-1)^{m-1}$ to
$\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)$ and the factor $(-1)^m\prod_iZ[k_i,\sigma(k_i)]$ to the product, in total $-\prod_iZ[k_i,\sigma(k_i)]$.
For each fixed point $k$ of $\sigma$ we replace $A[k,k]$ by the sum above and expand. The result is
\[
   \det A=\sum_{(f,C)}(-1)^{|C|}\prod_{k\in\mathcal N^\circ}Z[k,f(k)] ,
\]
where $f$ runs over the maps $\mathcal N^\circ\to\mathcal N$ without fixed points and $C$ runs over the sets of cycles of $f$. Here a
\emph{cycle} of $f$ is a subset $\{k_1,\dots,k_m\}$ of $\mathcal N^\circ$ with $m\ge2$ and $f(k_i)=k_{i+1}$ for all $i$
(indices modulo $m$); distinct cycles of $f$ are disjoint. Indeed, a permutation $\sigma$ together with the choices
made at its fixed points gives the pair $(f,C)$ in which $f$ is $\sigma$ on the cycles of $\sigma$ of length $\ge2$
and the chosen index at the fixed points, and $C$ is the set of these cycles; conversely $(f,C)$ determines $\sigma$,
which is $f$ on the union of the cycles in $C$ and the identity elsewhere, and the choices.

For a fixed $f$ the sum $\sum_C(-1)^{|C|}$ over all sets $C$ of cycles of $f$ is $1$ if $f$ has no cycle and $0$
otherwise. Finally, a map $f\colon\mathcal N^\circ\to\mathcal N$ without fixed points and without cycles is a tree rooted at $d$:
for $k\in\mathcal N^\circ$ the sequence $k,f(k),f(f(k)),\dots$ cannot stay in the finite set $\mathcal N^\circ$ for ever, because
its first repetition would produce a fixed point or a cycle; so it reaches $d$. Conversely a tree rooted at $d$ has
neither fixed points nor cycles.

label: def.trees
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def.trees}
An \emph{$a$-tree} is a map $\varphi$ from the set of edges different from $\hat e$ to the set of all edges such that
\[
   \varphi(o'_j)=o_j\qquad\text{and}\qquad\varphi(u'_j)\in\{u_j,o_j\}\qquad\text{for all crossings }j
\]
(as far as $o'_j$, resp.\ $u'_j$, is different from $\hat e$), and such that every edge different from $\hat e$ is mapped
to $\hat e$ by some iterate of $\varphi$. A \emph{$b$-tree} is a map $\psi$ from the set of edges different from $\hat e$
to the set of all edges such that
\[
   \psi(u_j)=u'_j\qquad\text{and}\qquad\psi(o_j)\in\{o'_j,u'_j\}\qquad\text{for all crossings }j
\]
(as far as $u_j$, resp.\ $o_j$, is different from $\hat e$), with the same condition on the iterates. For an $a$-tree
$\varphi$, a $b$-tree $\psi$ and a crossing $j$ we put
\[
  \vartheta_j(\varphi)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }\varphi(u'_j)=u_j,\\ 1&\text{if }\varphi(u'_j)=o_j,\\ \emptyset&\text{if }u'_j=\hat e,\end{cases}
  \qquad\qquad
  \vartheta_j(\psi)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }\psi(o_j)=o'_j,\\ 1&\text{if }\psi(o_j)=u'_j,\\ \emptyset&\text{if }o_j=\hat e.\end{cases}
\]
head: environment

label: prop.trees
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop.trees}
\begin{enumerate}\renewcommand{\roman{enumi}}{\roman{enumi}}
\item With $\varphi$ running over the $a$-trees and $\psi$ over the $b$-trees,
      \[
         P_w(x)=\sum_{\varphi}\ \prod_{j=1}^cp_{\vartheta_j(\varphi)}(x_j),\qquad
         \widetilde{P}_w(y)=\sum_{\psi}\ \prod_{j=1}^cp_{\vartheta_j(\psi)}(y_j).
      \]
\item With the sum running over all pairs of an $a$-tree $\varphi$ and a $b$-tree $\psi$,
      \[
         V_1(L;t_0,t_1)=(-1)^{\mu-1}\sum_{(\varphi,\psi)}\ \prod_{j=1}^cW_j\bigl(\vartheta_j(\varphi),\vartheta_j(\psi)\bigr),
      \]
      where the local weights
      $W_j(\vartheta,\vartheta')=\mathbbm E_{\bar x_j,\bar y_j}\bigl[p_{\vartheta}(x)\,p_{\vartheta'}(y)\bigr]$ are given by
      \[
        \renewcommand{1.2}{1.2}
        \begin{array}{c|ccc}
          W_j(\vartheta,\vartheta') & \vartheta'=0 & \vartheta'=1 & \vartheta'=\emptyset\\ \hline
          \vartheta=0 & 1 & \bar x_j-1 & \bar x_j\\
          \vartheta=1 & \bar y_j-1 & 2-\bar x_j-\bar y_j & 1-\bar x_j\\
          \vartheta=\emptyset & \bar y_j & 1-\bar y_j & 1
        \end{array}
      \]
\item For $\vartheta,\vartheta'\in\{0,1\}$,
      \[
         W_j(\vartheta,\vartheta')=p_\vartheta(\bar x_j)\,p_{\vartheta'}(\bar y_j)+(-1)^{\vartheta+\vartheta'}g_j ,
      \]
      and $W_j(\vartheta,\vartheta')=p_\vartheta(\bar x_j)\,p_{\vartheta'}(\bar y_j)$ if $\vartheta=\emptyset$ or
      $\vartheta'=\emptyset$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: pairs of spanning trees

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Every edge is the edge $o'_j$ or the edge $u'_j$ of exactly one crossing $j$. By Definition~\ref{def.T} the row
$o'_j$ of $T^a(x)$ has the single non-zero entry $1$ in the column $o_j$, and the row $u'_j$ has the entries $1-x_j$
in the column $o_j$ and $x_j$ in the column $u_j$. So the rows of $T^a(x)$ have sum $1$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem.mtt}, applied to $Z=T^a(x)$ and $d=\hat e$, gives
$\det((1-T^a(x))_{\hat e})=\sum_f\prod_{e\ne\hat e}T^a(x)[e,f(e)]$. The trees $f$ with a non-zero contribution are
exactly the $a$-trees $\varphi$, and the contribution of $\varphi$ is $\prod_jp_{\vartheta_j(\varphi)}(x_j)$. By
Proposition~\ref{prop.edge} the left-hand side is $P_w(x)$. In the same way, every edge is the edge $o_j$ or the edge
$u_j$ of exactly one crossing; the column $u_j$ of $T^b(y)$ has the single non-zero entry $1$ in the row $u'_j$, and
the column $o_j$ has the entries $y_j$ in the row $o'_j$ and $1-y_j$ in the row $u'_j$. So the transposed matrix
$Z=T^b(y)^{\mathsf{T}}$ satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem.mtt}, the trees with a non-zero contribution are the
$b$-trees, and $\widetilde{P}_w(y)=\det((1-T^b(y))_{\hat e})=\det((1-Z)_{\hat e})=\sum_\psi\prod_jp_{\vartheta_j(\psi)}(y_j)$.

(ii) By (i), $P_w(x)\widetilde{P}_w(y)=\sum_{(\varphi,\psi)}\prod_jp_{\vartheta_j(\varphi)}(x_j)\,p_{\vartheta_j(\psi)}(y_j)$, and the
$j$-th factor is a polynomial of degree $\le1$ in $x_j$ and in $y_j$ which involves no other variable. By
\eqref{eq.Emult}, $\mathbbm E$ of each product is $\prod_jW_j(\vartheta_j(\varphi),\vartheta_j(\psi))$, and the claim follows
from Theorem~\ref{thm.B}. The table is obtained from \eqref{eq.E1}: for instance
$\mathbbm E_{u,v}[(1-x)y]=v-1$ and $\mathbbm E_{u,v}[(1-x)(1-y)]=2-u-v$.

(iii) This is \eqref{eq.E1} again: $\mathbbm E_{u,v}[f]=f(u,v)+(1-uv)f_{11}$, and the coefficient of $xy$ in
$p_\vartheta(x)p_{\vartheta'}(y)$ is $(-1)^{\vartheta+\vartheta'}$ for $\vartheta,\vartheta'\in\{0,1\}$ and $0$ if one of
them is $\emptyset$.
head: environment

label: rem.trees
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem.trees}
By (iii), $V_1$ is the partition function of two spanning trees of the diagram which interact only at the crossings
where both of them have a choice: there the weight $p_\vartheta(\bar x_j)p_{\vartheta'}(\bar y_j)$ of the two independent
trees is changed by $+g_j$ if they make the same choice and by $-g_j$ if they make different choices. Without
this term, i.e.\ for $t_0t_1=1$, the state sum factors into $P_w(\bar x)\widetilde{P}_w(\bar y)$ by (i). For $x_j=t^{\varepsilon_j}$ the
weights $x_j$, $1-x_j$ are those of the random walk on the diagram which underlies the Burau representation, and (i)
is the corresponding expansion of the Alexander polynomial. These trees are in general more numerous than the
Kauffman states of the diagram: the closure of $\sigma_1^5$ has $11$ $a$-trees, whereas its diagram has $5$ Kauffman
states.

label: ex.trees
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex.trees}
Let $w=\sigma_1^3$, as in Example~\ref{ex.trefoil}. The six edges are the nodes $(p,j)$ with $p\in\{1,2\}$ and
$j\in\mathbbm Z/3$, and
\[
   (o_j,u_j,o'_j,u'_j)=\bigl((1,j),\,(2,j),\,(2,j+1),\,(1,j+1)\bigr),\qquad \hat e=(1,1)=o_1=u'_3 .
\]
So $\vartheta_3(\varphi)=\emptyset$ for every $a$-tree and $\vartheta_1(\psi)=\emptyset$ for every $b$-tree. There are
three $a$-trees, with $(\vartheta_1,\vartheta_2)=(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$: the fourth choice $(0,1)$ gives the cycle
$(1,2)\mapsto(2,1)\mapsto(1,3)\mapsto(1,2)$. Likewise there are three $b$-trees, with
$(\vartheta_2,\vartheta_3)=(0,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$. Hence
\[
   P_w=x_1x_2+(1-x_1)x_2+(1-x_1)(1-x_2),\qquad \widetilde{P}_w=y_2y_3+y_2(1-y_3)+(1-y_2)(1-y_3),
\]
in agreement with Example~\ref{ex.trefoil}. In the state sum (ii), the $a$-trees $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ contribute
$t_0\,\Sigma$ and $(1-t_0)\,\Sigma$ with $\Sigma=t_1+(1-t_1)+(t_0-1)(1-t_1)$, and the $a$-tree $(1,1)$ contributes
$(1-t_0)\bigl[(t_1-1)t_1+(t_1-1)(1-t_1)+(2-t_0-t_1)(1-t_1)\bigr]$. The sum of the nine terms is
\[
   V_1(3_1)=1-(1-t_0)(1-t_1)+(1-t_0)(1-t_1)(1-t_0-t_1)=1-(t_0+t_1)(1-t_0)(1-t_1).
\]

name: trefoil

label: thm.GHKSTp
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm.GHKSTp}
For $r=\pm1$ and $1\le p\le n$, the partial trace over all the tensor factors except the $p$-th one of the operator
$(h^{\otimes(p-1)}\otimes\mathrm{id}_W\otimes h^{\otimes(n-p)})\circ\varrho_r(w)$ is equal to $V_1(\widehat w)\,\mathrm{id}_W$. In particular
$V^{(p)}(w)=V_1(\widehat w)$.

label: prop.strandp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop.strandp}
Let $w$ be a braid word on $n$ strands with $c$ crossings and let $1\le p\le n$. Then
\[
   V^{(p)}(w)=(-1)^{n-1+c}\ \mathbbm E\Bigl[\det\bigl(1-B(x)^{(p)}\bigr)\,\det\bigl(1-\widetilde{B}(y)^{(p)}\bigr)\Bigr].
\]
Consequently, if $L$ is the closure of $w$, then for every $p$
\[
   V_1(L;t_0,t_1)=(-1)^{\mu-1}\ \mathbbm E\Bigl[\det\bigl(1-B(x)^{(p)}\bigr)\,\det\bigl(1-\widetilde{B}(y)^{(p)}\bigr)\Bigr].
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Steps~1 and~2 of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm.B} do not involve the first strand, and they give \eqref{eq.step2}.
In Step~3 we replace the set $Q$ by $Q_p=\{1,\dots,2n\}\smallsetminus\{2p-1,2p\}$, the set of the indices of the
basis vectors of $U_n$ other than $a_p$ and $b_p$. By \eqref{eq.Phi}, the vectors $e_I$ with $m_p=1$ correspond
under $\Phi_n$ to the $u_S$ with $S\subseteq Q_p$, and $\prod_{k\ne p}h_{m_k}=(-1)^{n-1}(-1)^{|S|}$ by
\eqref{eq.hparity}. Conjugation by the diagonal operator $K_n$ does not change diagonal matrix entries. Hence, by
\eqref{eq.step2}, Lemma~\ref{lem.compress} and the linearity of $\mathbbm E$,
\[
   V^{(p)}(w)=(-1)^{n-1+c}\sum_{S\subseteq Q_p}(-1)^{|S|}\,\mathbbm E\bigl[\langle u_S,{\textstyle\bigwedge}(\mathbbm B)u_S\rangle\bigr]
       =(-1)^{n-1+c}\,\mathbbm E\bigl[\det\bigl(1-\mathbbm B[Q_p|Q_p]\bigr)\bigr],
\]
where $\mathbbm B=B(x)\oplus\widetilde{B}(y)$. The matrix $\mathbbm B[Q_p|Q_p]$ is the endomorphism of the span of the $a_k,b_k$ with $k\ne p$
which acts by $B(x)^{(p)}$ on the $a_k$ and by $\widetilde{B}(y)^{(p)}$ on the $b_k$, so
$\det(1-\mathbbm B[Q_p|Q_p])=\det(1-B(x)^{(p)})\det(1-\widetilde{B}(y)^{(p)})$. The last statement follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm.GHKSTp} and from $(-1)^{n-1+c}=(-1)^{\mu-1}$, see \eqref{eq.VV1}.

label: prop.braidp
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The edge $\hat e$ contains a node $(p,j)$. The word $s_js_{j+1}\cdots s_cs_1\cdots s_{j-1}$ has the same closure diagram
as $w$, with the same edges and with the crossings renumbered, and the node $(p,j)$ of $w$ is the node $(p,1)$ of
this word. Since $\Upsilon(D_w,\hat e)$ does not depend on the numbering of the crossings, we may assume that $j=1$.

We repeat the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop.edge} with the node $(p,1)$ in place of the node $(1,1)$. In Step~1
the matrix $\Pi$ is replaced by the diagonal matrix $\Pi_p$ with the entry $0$ in the position $p$ and the entries
$1$ elsewhere, and one obtains
\[
   \det\bigl((1-\mathbbm T(x))_{\widehat{(p,1)}}\bigr)=\det\bigl(1-\Pi_p\,B(x)\,\Pi_p\bigr)=\det\bigl(1-B(x)^{(p)}\bigr).
\]
Step~2 is unchanged: the passive nodes are merged by Lemma~\ref{lem.merge}, and the deleted node $(p,1)$ becomes the
deleted edge $\hat e$. Hence $P_{D_w,\hat e}(x)=\det(1-B(x)^{(p)})$, and in the same way
$\widetilde{P}_{D_w,\hat e}(y)=\det(1-\widetilde{B}(y)^{(p)})$. The claim now follows from Proposition~\ref{prop.strandp}.

label: lem.elim
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.elim}
Let $Z$ be a square matrix with rows and columns indexed by a finite set $\mathcal N$, with entries in a commutative ring,
and let $\zeta\in\mathcal N$ be such that $Z[\zeta,\zeta]=0$. Let $Z^\natural$ be the matrix indexed by
$\mathcal N\smallsetminus\{\zeta\}$ with
\[
   Z^\natural[k,l]=Z[k,l]+Z[k,\zeta]\,Z[\zeta,l].
\]
Then $\det(1-Z)=\det(1-Z^\natural)$, and $\det\bigl((1-Z)_{\hat d}\bigr)=\det\bigl((1-Z^\natural)_{\hat d}\bigr)$ for every
$d\in\mathcal N$ different from $\zeta$.
head: environment
name: elimination of a node

title: Proof
body_md:
Order $\mathcal N$ so that $\zeta$ comes last. Then $1-Z=\begin{psmallmatrix}A&B\\D&1\end{psmallmatrix}$, where $A$ is the
matrix $1-Z$ restricted to $\mathcal N\smallsetminus\{\zeta\}$, $B$ is the column with the entries $-Z[k,\zeta]$ and $D$ is
the row with the entries $-Z[\zeta,l]$. By the identity
$\det\begin{psmallmatrix}A&B\\D&1\end{psmallmatrix}=\det(A-BD)$ used in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem.cyclic}, and since
$A-BD=1-Z^\natural$, we get the first claim. The second claim is the first one for the matrix obtained from $Z$ by
removing the row and the column of $d$, because this operation commutes with the passage from $Z$ to $Z^\natural$.
head: environment

label: lem.RII
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.RII}
Let $D^+$ be obtained from $D$ by a move of type~II in which $A$ passes over $B$. Let $\hat e$ be an edge of $D$ and
let $\hat e^+$ be the edge of $D^+$ defined by $\hat e^+=\hat e$ if $\hat e\notin\{A,B\}$, $\hat e^+=A_1$ if $\hat e=A$ and
$\hat e^+=B_1$ if $\hat e=B$. Then
\[
    \Upsilon(D^+,\hat e^+)=\Upsilon(D,\hat e).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We write $A,B$ for the edges $A_1,B_1$ of $D^+$, so that the edges of $D^+$ are the edges of $D$ and the four edges
$A_2,B_2,A_3,B_3$, and $\hat e^+=\hat e$. We write $x',x''$ for $x_{c+1},x_{c+2}$ and $y',y''$ for $y_{c+1},y_{c+2}$.

\smallskip\emph{The matrix $Z=T^a_{D^+}(x)$.} Let $k$ be an edge of $D$. The row $k$ of $Z$ is the row $k$ of
$T^a_D(x)$ in which the entries of the columns $A$ and $B$ have been moved to the columns $A_3$ and $B_3$; in
particular its entries in the columns $A,B,A_2,B_2$ are zero. The rows of the four other edges are, by the
definition of the edge matrices,
\begin{align*}
  Z[A_2,\cdot\,]&=e_A^{\mathsf{T}}, & Z[B_2,\cdot\,]&=(1-x')\,e_A^{\mathsf{T}}+x'e_B^{\mathsf{T}},\\
  Z[A_3,\cdot\,]&=e_{A_2}^{\mathsf{T}}, & Z[B_3,\cdot\,]&=(1-x'')\,e_{A_2}^{\mathsf{T}}+x''e_{B_2}^{\mathsf{T}}
\intertext{in the parallel case, and}
  Z[A_2,\cdot\,]&=e_A^{\mathsf{T}}, & Z[B_3,\cdot\,]&=(1-x')\,e_A^{\mathsf{T}}+x'e_{B_2}^{\mathsf{T}},\\
  Z[A_3,\cdot\,]&=e_{A_2}^{\mathsf{T}}, & Z[B_2,\cdot\,]&=(1-x'')\,e_{A_2}^{\mathsf{T}}+x''e_B^{\mathsf{T}}
\end{align*}
in the antiparallel case. We eliminate the node $A_2$ and then the node $B_2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem.elim}; this is
allowed because $Z[A_2,A_2]=Z[B_2,B_2]=Z[A_2,B_2]=0$. The rows of the edges of $D$ are not changed. In both cases the
rows $A_3$ and $B_3$ become
\begin{equation}\label{eq.bigon}
   e_A^{\mathsf{T}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad(1-X)\,e_A^{\mathsf{T}}+X\,e_B^{\mathsf{T}},\qquad\text{where }X=x'x'' ;
\end{equation}
for instance, in the parallel case the row $B_3$ becomes $(1-x'')e_A^{\mathsf{T}}+x''\bigl((1-x')e_A^{\mathsf{T}}+x'e_B^{\mathsf{T}}\bigr)$. So the
two new crossings act together as a single crossing with the parameter $x'x''$. Let $Z_1$ be the resulting matrix,
indexed by the edges of $D$ and by $A_3,B_3$. By Lemma~\ref{lem.elim}, $P_{D^+,\hat e}(x)=\det((1-Z_1)_{\hat e})$. The
matrix $Z_1$ is the sum of a matrix which does not involve $x',x''$ and of $X\,e_{B_3}(e_B-e_A)^{\mathsf{T}}$. So, by
Lemma~\ref{lem.rankone}, if $X$ is replaced by an indeterminate, then $\det((1-Z_1)_{\hat e})=p_0+X\,p_1$ with
polynomials $p_0,p_1$ in $x_1,\dots,x_c$, and therefore
\[
   P_{D^+,\hat e}(x)=p_0+x'x''\,p_1 .
\]
To compute $p_0+p_1$ we put $X=1$. The rows \eqref{eq.bigon} are then $e_A^{\mathsf{T}}$ and $e_B^{\mathsf{T}}$; in particular the
entries of $Z_1$ in the positions $(A_3,A_3)$, $(B_3,B_3)$ and $(A_3,B_3)$ are zero, so that we can eliminate the
node $A_3$ and then the node $B_3$ by Lemma~\ref{lem.elim}. This adds the columns $A_3$ and $B_3$ to the columns
$A$ and $B$ and removes the rows and the columns of $A_3$ and $B_3$, and we recover the matrix $T^a_D(x)$.
Hence $p_0+p_1=P_{D,\hat e}(x)$.

\smallskip\emph{The matrix $T^b_{D^+}(y)$.} The same computation applies. The rows of the new edges are now
$y'e_A^{\mathsf{T}}$, $(1-y')e_A^{\mathsf{T}}+e_B^{\mathsf{T}}$, $y''e_{A_2}^{\mathsf{T}}$, $(1-y'')e_{A_2}^{\mathsf{T}}+e_{B_2}^{\mathsf{T}}$ for $A_2,B_2,A_3,B_3$ in the parallel
case, and $y'e_A^{\mathsf{T}}$, $(1-y')e_A^{\mathsf{T}}+e_{B_2}^{\mathsf{T}}$, $y''e_{A_2}^{\mathsf{T}}$, $(1-y'')e_{A_2}^{\mathsf{T}}+e_B^{\mathsf{T}}$ for $A_2,B_3,A_3,B_2$ in the
antiparallel case. After the elimination of $A_2$ and $B_2$ the rows $A_3$ and $B_3$ are, in both cases,
\[
   Y\,e_A^{\mathsf{T}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad(1-Y)\,e_A^{\mathsf{T}}+e_B^{\mathsf{T}},\qquad\text{where }Y=y'y'' .
\]
The resulting matrix depends on $y',y''$ through the term $Y\,(e_{A_3}-e_{B_3})e_A^{\mathsf{T}}$ of rank one, and for $Y=1$ the
rows $A_3$ and $B_3$ are again $e_A^{\mathsf{T}}$ and $e_B^{\mathsf{T}}$, so that the elimination of $A_3$ and $B_3$ gives $T^b_D(y)$. Hence $\widetilde{P}_{D^+,\hat e}(y)=q_0+y'y''\,q_1$ with polynomials $q_0,q_1$ in
$y_1,\dots,y_c$ such that $q_0+q_1=\widetilde{P}_{D,\hat e}(y)$.

\smallskip\emph{The map $\mathbbm E$.} Let $m$ be a monomial in $x_1,\dots,x_c,y_1,\dots,y_c$ of degree $\le1$ in each
variable. By the definition \eqref{eq.E} and since $\varepsilon_{c+2}=-\varepsilon_{c+1}$,
\begin{gather*}
   \mathbbm E_{D^+}[x'x''m]=t_0^{\varepsilon}t_0^{-\varepsilon}\,\mathbbm E_D[m]=\mathbbm E_D[m],\qquad \mathbbm E_{D^+}[y'y''m]=t_1^{\varepsilon}t_1^{-\varepsilon}\,\mathbbm E_D[m]=\mathbbm E_D[m],\\
   \mathbbm E_{D^+}[x'x''y'y''m]=\mathbbm E_D[m].
\end{gather*}
Therefore
$\mathbbm E_{D^+}\bigl[(p_0+x'x''p_1)(q_0+y'y''q_1)\bigr]=\mathbbm E_D\bigl[(p_0+p_1)(q_0+q_1)\bigr]=\mathbbm E_D\bigl[P_{D,\hat e}\,\widetilde{P}_{D,\hat e}\bigr]$.

\smallskip\emph{The number of components.} By the combinatorial data of the two new crossings, the edge $A_1$ is
followed by $A_2$ and then by $A_3$ along its strand, and $B_1$ is followed by $B_2$ and then by $B_3$, in the
parallel case and in the antiparallel case. So the cycles of the permutation of Section~\ref{ssec.diagdef} for
$D^+$ are those for $D$ in which $A$ and $B$ have been replaced by $A_1,A_2,A_3$ and $B_1,B_2,B_3$, and the number
$\mu$ is the same for $D^+$ and for $D$. Hence $\Upsilon(D^+,\hat e^+)=\Upsilon(D,\hat e)$.

label: rem.RII
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem.RII}
The proof shows why $\mathbbm E$ is compatible with the moves of type~II: the two crossings of a bigon act as one
crossing with the parameters $x'x''$ and $y'y''$, this crossing acts trivially when both parameters are equal to
$1$, and $\mathbbm E$ sends $x'x''$, $y'y''$ and their product to $1$ because the two crossings have opposite signs. The
lemma does not use the fact that the diagrams are drawn on the sphere. Note that it says nothing about the cut
edges $A_2,B_2,A_3,B_3$ of $D^+$; these are covered by Theorem~\ref{thm.diagrams} below.

label: thm.vogel
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm.vogel}
Let $D$ be a diagram. There is a finite sequence $D=D_0,D_1,\dots,D_m$ of diagrams of the same link such that each
$D_{i+1}$ is obtained from $D_i$ by a Reidemeister move of type~II between two distinct edges of $D_i$, hence by a
move of type~II in the sense of Section~\ref{ssec.RII}, and such that $D_m$ is, up to an orientation-preserving
homeomorphism of $S^2$, the closure diagram $D_w$ of a braid word $w$.
head: environment
name: Yamada , Vogel

label: thm.diagrams
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm.diagrams}
Let $L$ be an oriented link with $\mu$ components, let $D$ be a connected diagram of $L$ with at least one crossing,
and let $\hat e$ be an edge of $D$. Then
\[
   V_1(L;t_0,t_1)=(-1)^{\mu-1}\ \mathbbm E_D\Bigl[\det\bigl((1-T^a_D(x))_{\hat e}\bigr)\,\det\bigl((1-T^b_D(y))_{\hat e}\bigr)\Bigr],
\]
where $\mathbbm E_D$ is the linear map with $\mathbbm E_D[x_j]=t_0^{\varepsilon_j}$, $\mathbbm E_D[y_j]=t_1^{\varepsilon_j}$ and $\mathbbm E_D[x_jy_j]=1$, multiplicative
over distinct crossings. In the notation \eqref{eq.Upsilon}: $V_1(L)=\Upsilon(D,\hat e)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $D=D_0,\dots,D_m$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm.vogel}. Put $\hat e_0=\hat e$ and let $\hat e_{i+1}=(\hat e_i)^+$ be the edge
of $D_{i+1}$ associated with the edge $\hat e_i$ of $D_i$ in Lemma~\ref{lem.RII}. By this lemma,
$\Upsilon(D_{i+1},\hat e_{i+1})=\Upsilon(D_i,\hat e_i)$ for all $i$, hence $\Upsilon(D,\hat e)=\Upsilon(D_m,\hat e_m)$. The diagram
$D_m$ has the same combinatorial data as the closure diagram $D_w$ of a braid word $w$ in which every position is
moved, and $\Upsilon$ depends only on the combinatorial data. All the $D_i$ are diagrams of $L$, so $L$ is the closure
of $w$, and $\Upsilon(D_m,\hat e_m)=V_1(L)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop.braidp}.

label: def.alttrees
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def.alttrees}
An \emph{under-tree} of $(D,\hat e)$ is a map $\tau$ which assigns to every crossing $j$ one of the two edges of the
under-strand at $j$, that is $\tau(j)\in\{u_j,u'_j\}$, with the following property. Let $f_\tau(j)=*$ if $\tau(j)=\hat e$, and
otherwise let $f_\tau(j)$ be the crossing at the other end of the edge $\tau(j)$: the crossing which $\tau(j)$ leaves if
$\tau(j)=u_j$, and the crossing which it enters if $\tau(j)=u'_j$. Then every crossing is mapped to $*$ by some iterate of
$f_\tau$. We put $S(\tau)=\{j:\tau(j)=u_j\}$.

An \emph{over-tree} of $(D,\hat e)$ is a map $\tau'$ which assigns to every crossing $j$ one of the two edges of the
over-strand at $j$, that is $\tau'(j)\in\{o_j,o'_j\}$, with the same property for the map $f_{\tau'}$ defined in the same
way: $f_{\tau'}(j)=*$ if $\tau'(j)=\hat e$, and otherwise $f_{\tau'}(j)$ is the crossing at the other end of $\tau'(j)$. We put
$S'(\tau')=\{j:\tau'(j)=o'_j\}$.

label: thm.positive
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm.positive}
Let $L$ be a link with $\mu$ components, let $D$ be a connected alternating diagram of $L$ with at least one
crossing, and let $\hat e$ be an edge of $D$ which leaves a crossing as its over-strand. Then
\[
   (-1)^{\mu-1}\,V_1(L;-t_0,-t_1)\;=\;\sum_{(\tau,\tau')}\ \ \prod_{j\in S(\tau)\smallsetminus S'(\tau')}t_0^{\varepsilon_j}
        \prod_{j\in S'(\tau')\smallsetminus S(\tau)}t_1^{\varepsilon_j},
\]
where the sum runs over all pairs of an under-tree $\tau$ and an over-tree $\tau'$ of $(D,\hat e)$. There is at least one
such pair. Thus the coefficient of $t_0^it_1^k$ in $(-1)^{\mu-1}V_1(L;-t_0,-t_1)$ is the number of pairs $(\tau,\tau')$ such
that $\sum_{j\in S(\tau)\smallsetminus S'(\tau')}\varepsilon_j=i$ and $\sum_{j\in S'(\tau')\smallsetminus S(\tau)}\varepsilon_j=k$.

label: ex.alttrefoil
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex.alttrefoil}
Let $D$ be the closure diagram of $\sigma_1^3$, with the notation of Example~\ref{ex.trees}: the edges are the nodes
$(p,j)$ with $p\in\{1,2\}$, $j\in\mathbbm Z/3$, and $(o_j,u_j,o'_j,u'_j)=((1,j),(2,j),(2,j+1),(1,j+1))$. The diagram is alternating,
$\mathcal E_{\rm I}$ consists of the edges $(2,j)$ and $\mathcal E_{\rm II}$ of the edges $(1,j)$. Take $\hat e=(2,1)=u_1=o'_3$, so that
$k_0=1$ and $j_1=3$. For an under-tree, $f_\tau(j)$ is $j+1$ if $\tau(j)=u'_j$ and $j-1$ if $\tau(j)=u_j$, except that
$f_\tau(1)=*$ if $\tau(1)=u_1$. The root $*$ can only be reached from the crossing $1$, so $\tau(1)=u_1$; of the four choices
at the crossings $2$ and $3$ only $\tau(2)=u'_2$, $\tau(3)=u_3$ is excluded, because it gives the cycle $2\mapsto3\mapsto2$.
So there are three under-trees, with $S(\tau)=\{1\}$, $\{1,2\}$, $\{1,2,3\}$. Likewise $f_{\tau'}(j)$ is $j-1$ if
$\tau'(j)=o_j$ and $j+1$ if $\tau'(j)=o'_j$, except that $f_{\tau'}(3)=*$ if $\tau'(3)=o'_3$, and there are three over-trees, with
$S'(\tau')=\{3\}$, $\{2,3\}$, $\{1,2,3\}$. All the crossings are positive, and the nine pairs contribute
\[
  t_0t_1+t_0t_1^2+t_1^2\;+\;t_0^2t_1+t_0t_1+t_1\;+\;t_0^2+t_0+1
     \;=\;V_1(3_1;-t_0,-t_1),
\]
in agreement with Example~\ref{ex.trefoil}.

label: prop.crowell
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop.crowell}
Let $D$ be a connected alternating diagram with $c\ge1$ crossings and let $\hat e\in\mathcal E_{\rm I}$. Then
\[
   P_{D,\hat e}(x)=(-1)^c\mathrm{sgn}(\mathsf n)\sum_{\tau}\ \prod_{j\in S(\tau)}(-x_j),\qquad
   \widetilde{P}_{D,\hat e}(y)=(-1)^c\mathrm{sgn}(\mathsf n)\sum_{\tau'}\ \prod_{j\in S'(\tau')}(-y_j),
\]
where $\tau$ runs over the under-trees and $\tau'$ over the over-trees of $(D,\hat e)$. Moreover $(D,\hat e)$ has at least
one under-tree and at least one over-tree.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Step 1: elimination of the edges of $\mathcal E_{\rm I}$.} Let $Z$ be the matrix $T^a_D(x)$ with the row and the column
of $\hat e$ removed, so that $P_{D,\hat e}(x)=\det(1-Z)$. By the definition of $T^a_D$, the rows of $Z$ are
\[
   Z[o'_j,\cdot\,]=e_{o_j}^{\mathsf{T}}\quad(o'_j\ne\hat e),\qquad\qquad Z[u'_j,\cdot\,]=(1-x_j)\,e_{o_j}^{\mathsf{T}}+x_j\,e_{u_j}^{\mathsf{T}},
\]
where the term $x_je_{u_j}^{\mathsf{T}}$ is absent if $u_j=\hat e$, that is, if $j=k_0$. The rows of the edges of $\mathcal E_{\rm I}$ have
their only non-zero entry in a column of $\mathcal E_{\rm II}$. We eliminate the nodes of $\mathcal E_{\rm I}\smallsetminus\{\hat e\}$ one
after the other by Lemma~\ref{lem.elim}. The elimination of $\zeta\in\mathcal E_{\rm I}$ adds $Z[k,\zeta]Z[\zeta,l]$ to the entry
$Z[k,l]$; this is non-zero only if $k,l\in\mathcal E_{\rm II}$, so the rows of the remaining edges of $\mathcal E_{\rm I}$ are not
changed and their diagonal entries remain zero. Since $u_j=o'_{\mathsf m^{-1}(j)}$, we end up with the matrix
$Z_{\rm II}$ indexed by $\mathcal E_{\rm II}$ whose rows are
\[
   Z_{\rm II}[u'_j,\cdot\,]=(1-x_j)\,e_{o_j}^{\mathsf{T}}+x_j\,e_{o_{\mathsf m^{-1}(j)}}^{\mathsf{T}}\qquad(\text{the last term is absent if }j=k_0),
\]
and $P_{D,\hat e}(x)=\det(1-Z_{\rm II})$.

\smallskip\emph{Step 2: a Laplacian.} We index the rows and the columns of $1-Z_{\rm II}$ by the crossings, the
crossing $l$ standing for the edge $o_l$. The row of the edge $u'_j=o_{\mathsf n(j)}$ is then the row $\mathsf n(j)$, and
it is $e_{\mathsf n(j)}^{\mathsf{T}}-(1-x_j)e_j^{\mathsf{T}}-x_je_{\mathsf m^{-1}(j)}^{\mathsf{T}}$. Let $\Lambda$ be the $c\times c$ matrix whose row $j$ is
minus the row $\mathsf n(j)$ of $1-Z_{\rm II}$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq.Lambda}
   \Lambda[j,\cdot\,]=(1-x_j)\,e_j^{\mathsf{T}}-e_{\mathsf n(j)}^{\mathsf{T}}+x_j\,e_{\mathsf m^{-1}(j)}^{\mathsf{T}}\qquad(\text{the last term is absent if }j=k_0).
\end{equation}
Then $\Lambda=-\mathsf N\,(1-Z_{\rm II})$, where $\mathsf N$ is the permutation matrix with $\mathsf N[j,\mathsf n(j)]=1$ for
all $j$, and therefore $P_{D,\hat e}(x)=\det(1-Z_{\rm II})=(-1)^c\mathrm{sgn}(\mathsf n)\det\Lambda$.

\smallskip\emph{Step 3: the matrix-tree theorem.} By Definition~\ref{def.alttrees}, the crossing at the other end of
$u'_j$ is $\mathsf n(j)$ and the crossing at the other end of $u_j$ is $\mathsf m^{-1}(j)$. We give the weight $1$ to the
edge $u'_j$ and the weight $-x_j$ to the edge $u_j$. For a crossing $j$ and $l\in\{1,\dots,c,*\}$ let $\mathsf w_j(l)$ be
the sum of the weights of the edges $e\in\{u'_j,u_j\}$ which lead from $j$ to $l$; here $u'_j$ leads to $\mathsf n(j)$,
and $u_j$ leads to $\mathsf m^{-1}(j)$ if $j\ne k_0$ and to $*$ if $j=k_0$. Thus $\sum_l\mathsf w_j(l)=1-x_j$, and by
\eqref{eq.Lambda} $\Lambda[j,l]=(1-x_j)\delta_{jl}-\mathsf w_j(l)$ for $l\ne*$; this also holds when two of the crossings $j$,
$\mathsf n(j)$, $\mathsf m^{-1}(j)$ coincide. We work over the field of rational functions in $x_1,\dots,x_c$. Let $Z^*$ be
the matrix indexed by $\{1,\dots,c,*\}$ with $Z^*[j,l]=\mathsf w_j(l)/(1-x_j)$ and with the row of $*$ equal to zero. Its
rows other than the row of $*$ have sum $1$, and $(1-Z^*)_{\hat *}$ is the matrix $\Lambda$ with its row $j$ divided by
$1-x_j$, for every $j$. By Lemma~\ref{lem.mtt},
\[
   \det\Lambda=\prod_{j=1}^c(1-x_j)\,\det\bigl((1-Z^*)_{\hat *}\bigr)=\sum_f\ \prod_{j=1}^c\mathsf w_j(f(j)),
\]
where $f$ runs over the trees rooted at $*$. Expanding each $\mathsf w_j(f(j))$ as a sum over the edges
$\tau(j)\in\{u'_j,u_j\}$ which lead from $j$ to $f(j)$, we obtain the sum over all maps $\tau$ such that $f_\tau$ is a tree
rooted at $*$, that is, over the under-trees, of the products $\prod_{j\in S(\tau)}(-x_j)$. This proves the formula for
$P_{D,\hat e}$.

\smallskip\emph{Step 4: the polynomial $\widetilde{P}_{D,\hat e}$.} A matrix and its transpose have the same determinant, so
$\widetilde{P}_{D,\hat e}(y)=\det(1-Z)$, where now $Z$ is the transpose of the matrix $T^b_D(y)$ with the row and the column of
$\hat e$ removed. By the definition of $T^b_D$, the rows of $Z$ are
\[
   Z[u_j,\cdot\,]=e_{u'_j}^{\mathsf{T}}\quad(u_j\ne\hat e),\qquad\qquad Z[o_j,\cdot\,]=(1-y_j)\,e_{u'_j}^{\mathsf{T}}+y_j\,e_{o'_j}^{\mathsf{T}},
\]
where the term $y_je_{o'_j}^{\mathsf{T}}$ is absent if $o'_j=\hat e$, that is, if $j=j_1$. The situation is the same as in Step~1,
with the roles of the over-strands and of the under-strands exchanged: the rows of the edges of $\mathcal E_{\rm I}$ have
their only non-zero entry in a column of $\mathcal E_{\rm II}$. Eliminating the edges of $\mathcal E_{\rm I}\smallsetminus\{\hat e\}$, and
using $o'_j=u_{\mathsf m(j)}$, we obtain the matrix indexed by $\mathcal E_{\rm II}$ with the rows
$(1-y_j)e_{u'_j}^{\mathsf{T}}+y_je_{u'_{\mathsf m(j)}}^{\mathsf{T}}$ for the edges $o_j$, where the last term is absent if $j=j_1$. We now let
the crossing $l$ stand for the edge $u'_l$; the edge $o_j=u'_{\mathsf n^{-1}(j)}$ is then the row $\mathsf n^{-1}(j)$. With
\[
   \Lambda'[j,\cdot\,]=(1-y_j)\,e_j^{\mathsf{T}}-e_{\mathsf n^{-1}(j)}^{\mathsf{T}}+y_j\,e_{\mathsf m(j)}^{\mathsf{T}}\qquad(\text{the last term is absent if }j=j_1)
\]
we get, as in Step~2, $\widetilde{P}_{D,\hat e}(y)=(-1)^c\mathrm{sgn}(\mathsf n^{-1})\det\Lambda'=(-1)^c\mathrm{sgn}(\mathsf n)\det\Lambda'$. The crossing
at the other end of $o_j$ is $\mathsf n^{-1}(j)$ and the crossing at the other end of $o'_j$ is $\mathsf m(j)$, so Step~3,
with the weight $1$ for $o_j$ and the weight $-y_j$ for $o'_j$, gives
$\det\Lambda'=\sum_{\tau'}\prod_{j\in S'(\tau')}(-y_j)$.

\smallskip\emph{Step 5: existence of trees.} Direct every edge of $D$ from the crossing at which it is the
under-strand to the crossing at which it is the over-strand. In the directed graph obtained in this way, whose
vertices are the crossings, two arcs start at every vertex (the edges $u_j,u'_j$) and two arcs end at every vertex
(the edges $o_j,o'_j$). Let $\mathcal R$ be the set of the crossings from which there is a directed path to $k_0$.
No arc leads from the complement of $\mathcal R$ to $\mathcal R$. So the $2\,|\mathcal R^c|$ arcs which start in
$\mathcal R^c$ also end in $\mathcal R^c$; since exactly $2\,|\mathcal R^c|$ arcs end in $\mathcal R^c$, no arc leads
from $\mathcal R$ to $\mathcal R^c$ either. As $D$ is connected and $k_0\in\mathcal R$, every crossing belongs to
$\mathcal R$. Now let $\tau(k_0)=\hat e$, and for $j\ne k_0$ let $\tau(j)$ be the first arc of a directed path of minimal
length from $j$ to $k_0$. Then $f_\tau(j)$ is closer to $k_0$ than $j$ for $j\ne k_0$, and $f_\tau(k_0)=*$, so $\tau$ is an
under-tree. Reversing all the arcs and replacing $k_0$ by $j_1$, we find an over-tree in the same way.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm.diagrams},
\[
   V_1(L;t_0,t_1)=(-1)^{\mu-1}\,\mathbbm E_D\bigl[P_{D,\hat e}(x)\,\widetilde{P}_{D,\hat e}(y)\bigr].
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop.crowell}, in which the two signs $(-1)^c\mathrm{sgn}(\mathsf n)$ cancel,
\[
   P_{D,\hat e}(x)\,\widetilde{P}_{D,\hat e}(y)=\sum_{(\tau,\tau')}\ \prod_{j\in S(\tau)}(-x_j)\prod_{j\in S'(\tau')}(-y_j).
\]
Let $S=S(\tau)$ and $S'=S'(\tau')$. By the definition \eqref{eq.E} of $\mathbbm E_D$, and since $|S|+|S'|$ and
$|S\smallsetminus S'|+|S'\smallsetminus S|$ have the same parity,
\[
   \mathbbm E_D\Bigl[\,\prod_{j\in S}(-x_j)\prod_{j\in S'}(-y_j)\Bigr]
     =\prod_{j\in S\smallsetminus S'}\bigl(-t_0^{\varepsilon_j}\bigr)\prod_{j\in S'\smallsetminus S}\bigl(-t_1^{\varepsilon_j}\bigr)
     =\prod_{j\in S\smallsetminus S'}(-t_0)^{\varepsilon_j}\prod_{j\in S'\smallsetminus S}(-t_1)^{\varepsilon_j},
\]
because $-t^{\varepsilon}=(-t)^{\varepsilon}$ for $\varepsilon=\pm1$. Hence
\[
   V_1(L;t_0,t_1)=(-1)^{\mu-1}\sum_{(\tau,\tau')}\ \prod_{j\in S(\tau)\smallsetminus S'(\tau')}(-t_0)^{\varepsilon_j}
        \prod_{j\in S'(\tau')\smallsetminus S(\tau)}(-t_1)^{\varepsilon_j},
\]
and the formula of the theorem follows by replacing $t_0,t_1$ by $-t_0,-t_1$. The set of pairs is not empty by the
last statement of Proposition~\ref{prop.crowell}.

label: lem.split
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem.split}
If $L$ is a split link, then $V_1(L)=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $L$ be the union of two links $L_1$ and $L_2$ which are separated by a sphere. By Alexander's theorem, $L_1$
and $L_2$ are the closures of braid words $w_1$ and $w_2$ on $n_1$ and $n_2$ strands, and $L$ is the closure of the
word $w$ on $n_1+n_2$ strands obtained by placing $w_2$ to the right of $w_1$; no letter of $w$ is $\sigma_{n_1}^{\pm1}$.
Hence the matrix $B(x)$ of \eqref{eq.B} is block diagonal, $B(x)=B_1\oplus B_2$ with blocks of sizes $n_1$ and $n_2$, and
$1-B(x)'=(1-B_1')\oplus(1-B_2)$. Each of the matrices $\rho(x_j)$, $\rho^-(x_j)$ fixes the vector $(1,1)^{\mathsf{T}}$, so $B_2$ fixes
the vector $(1,\dots,1)^{\mathsf{T}}$ and $\det(1-B_2)=0$. Therefore $P_w=0$, and $V_1(L)=0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm.B}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $D$ be an alternating diagram of $L$. If $D$ is not connected, then $L$ is a split link and $V_1(L)=0$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem.split}. If $D$ is connected and has no crossing, then $L$ is the unknot and $V_1(L)=1$
(Example~\ref{ex.unknot}). If $D$ is connected and has at least one crossing, then $\mathcal E_{\rm I}$ is not empty, and
Theorem~\ref{thm.positive} shows that $(-1)^{\mu-1}V_1(L;-t_0,-t_1)$ is a non-empty sum of monomials with coefficient
$1$; in particular its coefficients are non-negative and it is not zero. Finally, the coefficient of $t_0^it_1^k$ in
$V_1(L;-t_0,-t_1)$ is $(-1)^{i+k}$ times the coefficient of $t_0^it_1^k$ in $V_1(L;t_0,t_1)$.

label: rem.altcomments
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem.altcomments}
\begin{enumerate}\renewcommand{\roman{enumi}}{\roman{enumi}}
\item \emph{The number of terms.} For $t_0=t_1=1$, Theorem~\ref{thm.positive} says that $(-1)^{\mu-1}V_1(L;-1,-1)$ is
      the number of under-trees times the number of over-trees. By Proposition~\ref{prop.crowell} these two
      numbers are $|P_{D,\hat e}|$ and $|\widetilde{P}_{D,\hat e}|$ at $x_j=y_j=-1$. 
\item \emph{The Alexander polynomial.} For $x_j=t^{\varepsilon_j}$, Proposition~\ref{prop.crowell} gives
      \[
         P_{D,\hat e}(t^{\varepsilon})=\pm\sum_\tau\ \prod_{j\in S(\tau)}(-t)^{\varepsilon_j}.
      \]
      Together with the classical fact that $P_{D,\hat e}(t^{\varepsilon})$ is
      the Alexander polynomial of $L$ up to a sign and a power of $t$ (compare Remark~\ref{rem.burau}), this is the
      theorem that the Alexander polynomial of an alternating link is alternating, which is due to Crowell
      \cite{Crowell} and, for knots, to Murasugi \cite{Murasugi}. Theorem~\ref{thm.positive} is the same statement for two coupled copies: the map
      $\mathbbm E_D$ preserves the signs because it sends $(-x_j)(-y_j)$ to $1$.
\item \emph{Regarding the hypothesis.} The diagram has to be alternating in Proposition~\ref{prop.crowell}. For the closure
      diagram of $w=\sigma_1^3\sigma_2\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_2$, a non-alternating diagram of the knot $5_2$, the polynomial $P_w$
      contains the monomials $1$ and $-x_1x_2x_3x_5$, which have opposite signs as monomials in the $-x_j$. And for
      the closure of $(\sigma_1\sigma_2)^4$, the non-alternating knot $8_{19}$, the polynomial $V_1$ contains the monomials
      $1$ and $t_1^3$ with the coefficient $+1$, so it is not alternating.
\end{enumerate}
